utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that you have given me the floor, just two brief matters. Once Mr. Moore is in the courtroom, and I think he's scheduled to examine the next witness, then perhaps once we conclude the examination of Mr. Panic, we could discuss an issue that I wanted to raise. Another matter is timekeeping. I pay great attention to the time we spent with each witness. Mr. Weiner said that he would need another hour for this witness, and I know that I took almost a day less ten minutes, and also bearing in mind the examination of Mr. Vasic, I would simply like to -- everybody to be careful with time because we have the next witness here, and I will have quite a bit to cover in my redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have opened up a subject that is dear to our heart. We're watching closely as well the time taken with each witness and people are stretching out their time. We are going to fall behind if that happens. We will have to watch and act if people just take too long. There is always another issue that can be looked at on the facts, because almost every fact has at least three different versions of it. Most of them are not going to determine the outcome of this case. So attention needs to be paid to the points that matter and deal with those within time and then we will have a hope of finishing this case. Sir, may I remind you of the affirmation you made which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I hope you're stimulated to finish more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I am set to go, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go over -- good afternoon first.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would like to go over an area which we discussed last week concerning Ovcara, and just based on your answers that you gave, I just want to cover a few matters within that. You said you arrived at Ovcara and you stayed for approximately, is it 15 minutes to one half hour?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then you said that -- you did indicate -- approximately what time did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at around 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said that you met with Colonel Mrksic at approximately 3.30?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you think you had been in Ovcara from approximately 2.45 to approximately 3.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I spent some 15 minutes at Ovcara and the rest was spent travelling or in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, were you at Ovcara approximately from 3.00 to 3.15 p.m., 1500 hours to 1515 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's been a long time. I really couldn't say. I know that I spent about 15 minutes, but I couldn't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, there's been testimony in this case that the buses arrived around 2.00 p.m., at pages 7703 was the testimony, and that the beatings took one hour to one and a half hours, at page 5018. Based on your testimony, you had to have been present when the beatings occurred.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I came at the end when the buses were already turning back to go to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified that Colonel Vojnovic told you about the gauntlet. Do you agree that there was no other person who told you about that gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic told me something about it very briefly, but he told me much more at the military court, and later on, when testifying before the special court at the trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But Colonel Vojnovic was the only person that you learned about the gauntlet from; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on Friday, you testified first at page 14464 that the gauntlet was used to settle accounts. And then you said you wanted to give a full description is what you heard from Colonel Vojnovic. And you indicated that at page 14466: "The gauntlet was used as a tool for identification." Which was it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People wanted to see who was on the opposite side, they wanted to recognise them, and there were attempts to take revenge in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you've never heard in your lifetime of an identification gauntlet from anyone, prior to your testimony on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a typical case of identification. What Vojnovic told me was that there were people who tried to recognise whether any of those on the opposite side had killed some of their family members in the most brutal way. At any rate, they were trying to find ways to identify those who had done that to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that prior to this testimony, you've never in your lifetime heard of something called an identification gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would neither agree with it nor would I accept it as a method of identification. Perhaps the meaning of the uttered words is different but the essence is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, are you aware that Colonel Vojnovic has denied ever seeing you at Ovcara? And that's at 8842, 8946 of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he stated that, then that's based on his observation. I don't think that he could have forgotten me. We met, and I have witnesses who can testify about us meeting at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel Vojnovic has testified that he met you at the Belgrade trial and was surprised when you told him that you were there. That was the first time he'd ever heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's due to the passage of time. Perhaps he has indeed forgotten or perhaps he has some other problems. If necessary, I can direct you to people who can testify about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you didn't learn about the gauntlet from Colonel Vojnovic, there's only one way you could have learned, that you were present for that. You were present when those beatings occurred; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is your right to draw that type of conclusion, but it is not correct. I wasn't there at the time of the beatings, that's the first fact. The second one is that I met with Colonel Vojnovic there, we talked, and I told you here what we had talked about. I repeat I can give you the names of other persons who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. You gave a statement over a two-day period to the Office of the Prosecutor; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that it was given not at the ICTY offices but on both days, or actually all three days, it was given at the VG Dom; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the VJ Dom is part of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you originally met for two days in July to give that statement, and when it was completed you would not sign the English copy because you wanted to review it in the Serbian language; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the -- your request was honoured and your remarks were translated into Serbian, and five weeks later they returned and showed you the statement in Serbian; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you met on September 1st, 2005, with two people from the Office of the Prosecutor and a translator; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was at the time when I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you recall that when you were first shown the document to review you didn't read it in haste but you spent hours reviewing that statement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly hours, but until I've read it through. Because there were hundreds of answers and three times as many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that you reviewed that statement for two to three hours; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that you made corrections on almost every page of that document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because there were both mistakes in terms of content, style, language, typographical errors, and so on, and we corrected that together, and I'm sure that there are some that are still there. However, I accept the document as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, can I just show you the English version with the corrections, may I show the Court, and just show you how extensive those corrections were. Sir, I just want to show you this. When you made the statements in Serbian, the corrections had to be made in English, and I just want to show the extent of the corrections. You indicated that you accept the document as a whole, but I just want to show you -- show the Court and yourself the extent of the corrections you made. If you look at page 2, there's a few corrections because they had to change the English when you changed the Serbian. Page 3, there's lots of corrections; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you also note on page 3 right by paragraph 14 there's a time, 9.40? To the left of paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you remember all these corrections being made, large numbers of corrections, don't you, being made?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if we move to page 4, again, we see large numbers of corrections, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there's also a time by paragraph 17 to the left in the column, 9.51?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you made all these corrections because you wanted it to be right, you wanted it to be correct and true; isn't that certain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I did not speak English, so we had to do it together. I think it was done with the best of intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, page 5, we see a number of corrections made again. And by page -- do you see a number of corrections are made again? And by paragraph 23, we see the time 10.02.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And again, I say to you these corrections were made because you wanted an accurate statement to be produced; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 6, just a few corrections. Page 7, just a few corrections again, but there's a time listed by paragraph 35, 10.26. Continuing to page 8, no corrections on that page. There's a time at 10.30 listed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 9 has only two corrections. And if we look at pages 11 -- I'm sorry, 10, 11, just a few corrections per page. Is that correct, sir? Just a few corrections per page?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if you notice at the top of page 11, right by -- right above paragraph 56 it says 10.40.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you start at 9.00, that session, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you've now been there for an hour and 40 minutes. Now, if we go to page 12, a few more corrections?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you crossed out a line. On paragraph 64, you crossed out the final line; isn't that correct? Or it's crossed out in the English.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Page 13 has a few corrections. Page 14 has no corrections. Page 15. Page 15 has several corrections. In fact, you changed -- in paragraph 79, you made a change. Initially, the statement read: "There were no civilian police in Vukovar prior to 20 November 1991, nor any other functioning civilian public service." And you changed that to, the new paragraph would read, the last sentence: "I am not aware of the existence of a functioning civil police or any other civil service in Vukovar before the departure of the Guards Motorised Brigade from Vukovar on 24 November 1991." Do you recall that change?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And both versions could remain. It doesn't change the true meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you can see from this page -- there were several corrections made on that page, almost -- the last three paragraphs have lots of corrections. That's on page 15.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if we go to page 16, paragraph 80, you crossed out that whole top -- that whole portion that's on the top of page 16. You deleted that whole section. It went from -- if you even look in the Serbian version, from a long paragraph to a very short paragraph in just a few sentences; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you'll also notice on page - excuse me, sorry - on page 16, there are two times listed, 10.23 -- I'm sorry, 11.23, and 11.31.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And below that is 11.31.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the next page, there are a few changes, page 17.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And page 18, there's a number of changes. And in paragraph 92, you changed that final sentence of that paragraph which originally was, in that paragraph: "If Vojnovic withdrew his," something "MPs without the approval" -- it originally said TO; then it was changed to MP. But it said: "If Vojnovic withdrew his MPs without the approval of Mrksic, this would be a violation of the regulations." And you changed that paragraph to: "It is possible that somebody carried out the withdrawal of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade without Mrksic's authorisation, but this would represent a violation of regulations." Do you remember making that change?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because this was not the TO police, it was the police of the 80th Brigade, so that was the factual mistake, but otherwise it's the same. Nobody can pull out the police units without the consent of the brigade commander or their superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And finally on pages 19 and 20, no changes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said after you completed this, you said on page 7, you accepted this document as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, after all the changes came in, a new printed copy was given to you to sign with all of those changes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after reviewing that, you even made a change on page 4 to that. That's in your -- that's in the final signed statement. Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you made another change on your final -- on the final version?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although this is immaterial, it's just a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, thereafter you signed every page?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you signed the first page as well as the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you signed on page 2 the first paragraph that you're giving this statement voluntarily "and will describe everything I know to the best of my knowledge and recollection."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want you to turn to paragraph 72 on page 18. Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll read it: "It was unusual for a security officer to be given the responsibility for an evacuation operation. However, I assume Mrksic appointed Sljivancanin to the position because of the important role the security organ had to play in the operation. Sljivancanin was not only responsible for the selection of prisoners, he also commanded the entire evacuation of the people to Sremska Mitrovica. This implied that Sljivancanin was able to issue orders to the military police or any other unit participating in the operation." Now, sir, you said that. You said that to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you said it, not only did you say it, you signed below that at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And not only did you say Sljivancanin was responsible for the entire evacuation, you continue in paragraph 73, right below that. Do you have that paragraph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "I believe Sljivancanin went to the hospital on 19th November to prepare for his task, based on an entry in the war diary, ERN B/C/S 0293-5434 - 0293-5482, ERN English L010-0496 - L010-0537, GM TBR or Guards Motorised Brigade, 19th, 2000 hours, arrival of security officers to select and separate members of Ustasha units from civilians. The selection of prisoners began in the morning of 20th November. I do not know whether Sljivancanin issued any specific orders, verbal or written, regarding the organisation and implementation of evacuation. He must have been issuing orders to the military police." You also said that, sir, didn't you, and signed right below that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And twice, sir, you've indicated - last week - that paragraph 69 was correct. Twice in your testimony last week you've indicated that that was correct. And that is -- I'll just read the first few lines which is what we discussed: "Mrksic also informed us at the command briefing in Negoslavci on 19th November 1991," and you said that that happened -- it says 18th, but you say that happened on the 19th. "That Major Sljivancanin was going to be in charge, that is command, of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th and 20th November. Mrksic said Sljivancanin was allowed to use as many policemen as necessary to escort the prisoners and ensure their safe passage." Twice last week you said that was correct other than the date; it shouldn't read 18th but should read the 19th. Do you still agree to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the date is not the 18th. We got the order to free the hospital on the 19th. So it can't possibly be the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the -- you've said that you accept this document as a whole, and as stated, there's an acknowledgment on page 28 in the English, a witness acknowledgment on 28, and it should be 28 in your version. And it says: "I have read this statement ..."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What about the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's after the paragraphs; it's the witness acknowledgment section. It should be the last page where you sign at the end. It says "witness acknowledgment" at the top.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you stated that you have read this statement in the Serbo-Croatian language, and "it contains everything I said to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you further state: "I have given this statement voluntarily and am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." That's your signature.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all correct. But if I may, while preparing for my evidence and while talking to a number of persons, I became familiar of some new facts and new documents which would shed a somewhat different light on all of these. So if there is time, I would be willing to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you agree that everything you stated here you believe to be true in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, on those days, and given the situation in which I provided that statement, and my mental and physical state at the time, this is indeed what I stated. But, again, while preparing for this testimony, I became familiar with new documents and my memory was jogged in relation to a number of situations. And especially as I was following this trial, I realised that at some points, I was misled or confused or simply wrong or that I had given some persons assignments that they simply didn't have at the time, whereas I believed them to have those assignments and specific powers. The person I have in mind specifically is Major Sljivancanin. I realise that based on the documents, the evacuation --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finish.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may. Based on the documents available, it was Colonel Pavkovic who was in charge of the evacuation, while Major Sljivancanin was in charge of his security tasks. Security assessment, selection of those who were active fighters and those who had not been involved in the actual fighting. Yes, please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir you've testified in this case and given numerous statements from here to Novi Sad to Belgrade, and never, since 1998, have you ever, ever indicated that Major -- that Colonel Pavkovic was in charge of the evacuation; isn't that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Absolutely correct. But please allow me. It was only --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me finish. You've also stated that you were present when Colonel Mrksic appointed or tasked Major Sljivancanin to be in charge of the evacuation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I remembered. But the documents suggest otherwise, so these are new facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And those are documents shown to you by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are documents shown to me over these days as I was preparing for my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say these days when you were preparing for your evidence, are we talking about last week with Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also as I was preparing for my arrival and after I had arrived, a document turned up which indicates that he had been involved in the negotiations -- Colonel Pavkovic, that he received those people and that he led them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any document from a JNA commander appointing Colonel Pavkovic to command the evacuation? Are you in possession of any such document from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a document produced by the command of the 1st Military District and the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're saying this document appoints Colonel Pavkovic to command the evacuation? I'm aware of the document where he is sent to the Guards Motorised Brigade, but again, do you possess any document from the JNA command tasking or ordering Colonel Pavkovic to be in charge or in command of that evacuation? No one in this Court has ever seen such a document. Do you have one in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have one in my possession, but I did see the document talking about the involvement of Pavkovic, who would negotiating, receiving, and taking those people away. After all, he's right there in those recordings, but that's a bit of a special topic, isn't it? The answer is I don't have the document on me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The issue of his command, sir. You've already indicated that the paragraph in your statement is correct, that you were present when Colonel Mrksic appointed Major Sljivancanin to be in charge of that evacuation. You don't have any document in your possession from Colonel Mrksic indicating that Colonel Pavkovic was in charge of the evacuation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've never seen any such document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think Colonel Mrksic wrote the document -- or, rather, he didn't order for that document to be written. I don't think there was actually a document that was written in relation to that evacuation by Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know nowhere in the war diary does it say that Colonel Pavkovic was in charge of the evacuation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference in the war diary somewhere to the effect that Colonel Pavkovic received them, and I think there is also another reference to that in a report, the delegation of the International Red Cross, that he talked to them and that he came with them to implement that task. There is a reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you know he was involved in the Mitnica evacuation. And you know that the Red Cross was not present for the evacuation of that first group that left the hospital. So there was no negotiation about that first group with Colonel Pavkovic and the Red Cross. There is nothing, isn't that correct, in the war diary, indicating that Colonel Pavkovic was in charge of that evacuation from the hospital that eventually went to the barracks and then Ovcara. Would you like to review the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we don't quite have time for that now. But the International Red Cross were not at Mitnica but they were at the hospital, and Pavkovic was with them. That's true, you can see that in the recordings and you can see that in all the coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's clear in this case that that group that went to the barracks had left prior to the internationals arriving at the hospital, that the internationals weren't at the barracks while they were there, and that the internationals weren't at Ovcara. So again, do you have any documents indicating -- or aware of any documents from the JNA indicating that Colonel Pavkovic was in charge of that particular evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any such document. But let me say this: On the 19th when I was briefly at the hospital, there were people there from the International Red Cross outside the hospital. I saw at least one of them bearing the Red Cross insignia, as well as an unknown person in white.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not the question. We're dealing with the 20th, or we're dealing with documents. You know that the Red Cross was not present when those people were taken out of the hospital. They weren't present on those buses. They weren't present at the barracks, and they weren't present when they were beaten at Ovcara or when they were murdered at Ovcara. You know that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in the area on the 20th myself, not near the hospital, not inside the hospital; therefore, I can hardly be expected to talk about any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you were at Ovcara and at the barracks, you know that there was no one there from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I saw, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have no documents, there is nothing in the war diary relating to Colonel Pavkovic. I put to you, sir, that the only reason you have mentioned Colonel Pavkovic today was to remove responsibility for those crimes or was to attempt to remove responsibility for those crimes from the -- from Operations Group South, the Guards Motorised Brigade, and yourself, sir. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it's not. When I came here to testify, it was only because I wanted to be here myself, as well as others. I think we all care equally about discovering the truth and I think each of us should be individually responsible for whatever we did or failed to do. I am ready to take my share of the responsibility. I am not here to defend anyone or indeed blame anyone. That's not my objective. My objective is to have the truth out finally, after such a long time. As you see yourself, it is proving to be an arduous task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let me cover one more issue since you've agreed with everything in this document. You mention Colonel Mrksic in this document. Paragraph 92, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "In my opinion, the two central issues concerning Ovcara are: One, how long the JNA can secure the hangar. Two, why did the JNA leave the area. The order for the withdrawal of the military police could have been issued only by the commander of the military police of either the Guards Motorised Brigade or the 80th Motorised Brigade. As the commander of OG South, Colonel Mile Mrksic was the highest ranking commander in the area. This means the order of the JNA withdrawal must have been issued or at least authorised by him. I know Mrksic very well and cannot imagine he would have issued such an order. However, the order for withdrawal of military police could have only come from him. The military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade withdrew on JNA orders. They were not forced out by the local Serbian TO. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic could have issued the order for the withdrawal of the military police but not without consulting Mrksic. It is possible that someone carried out the withdrawal of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade without Mrksic's authorisation but that would represent a violation of the regulations." Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know, sir, that no charges were ever brought for withdrawing the military police without Mrksic's authorisation. No charges were ever brought by the Guards Motorised Brigade or the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So there being no alleged violation of regulations, Mrksic had to issue -- had to have issued the orders or authorised that order, is what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let the question be answered first, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since there was no allegations of violation of regulations in relation that someone acted without Mrksic's authorisation, the only answer is that Mrksic issued the order or authorised it, which is what you say in your statement here.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated -- or, rather, I'm trying to answer this for my own benefit. How did all of this come to happen, all these here are assumptions. On my part, however, I do believe that the Trial Chamber will sooner or later get to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, you've stated: "The order for the withdrawal of the military police could have only come from him," referring to Colonel Mrksic. "The military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade withdrew on JNA orders. They were not forced out by the local Serbian TO. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic could have issued the order for withdrawal but with not consulting Mrksic."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago, I wanted to raise an objection because the witness was being asked to speculate and the witness's answer clearly reflects that circumstance; whereas, now my learned friend Mr. Weiner quotes this order about the withdrawal of the military police, page 21, lines 15 and 16, Mr. Weiner actually said that the witness had stated in his original statement that the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade could only have been withdrawn pursuant to orders of Colonel Mrksic. If we look at item 92, we see the witness stating that the military police could have been pulled out by the commander of the military police, the Guards Brigade, or the 80th Brigade. I think that is essentially different from what Mr. Weiner has been putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You stated that "either Mrksic issued the order or Vojnovic issued the order but not without consulting Mrksic." Those are your words, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, that could have been done by the commander of the military police company without informing Vojnovic. Vojnovic could have done it without informing Mrksic. All of these are possibilities and I am -- most likely we will establish the facts. Our rules of subordination and singleness of command mandate that if somebody issued an order, he had to inform his superior officer regarding that; or, if he received an order from another person, he also had to inform his superior officer about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's -- you've just indicated that Vojnovic could have done it without informing Mrksic. Sir, you've stated here that: "Vojnovic could have issued the order for the withdrawal of the military police but not without consulting Mrksic." And you further stated that it would be a violation of regulations if he had done so without consulting Mrksic. Do you agree with that, sir? You're nodding your head, could you please ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to cover the area of resubordination which you mentioned very briefly in response to Mr. Borovic's questioning. You know, sir, that the resubordination of units is an important decision of a commander and it has to be in writing in some manner in a written order or it must be reflected in the war diary if it's given orally before the written order is issued.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that the war diary for the Guards Motorised Brigade and Operations Group South does not mention any resubordination of the TO or volunteer units prior to November 21st. And you said that at paragraph 97.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, are you aware that the summary of the war diary of the 1st Motorised battalion, which was provided to this Court, it's Exhibit 807, does not mention the resubordination of the volunteers or the TO.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't study it in detail, but I accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 415, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is the order of General Panic of November 18th. You've seen this document before, and you're familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just look at it. Could you move it, please? Yes, I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I just want to refer to two notes in this document. One is the second paragraph where it says: "The Croatian armed forces are defeated in the area." It should be the first paragraph in B/C/S -- I'm sorry, in Serbian. Do you see it on the top, "oruzane snage Hrvatske na prostoru"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Croatian forces are defeated in the area of combat operations carried out by the 1st VO units. However, the war did not end with the fall of Vukovar. An even more fierce and brutal war against Ustasha forces is ahead of us." You were aware, sir, at that time that there were still pockets of resistance and there was still fighting in Croatia occurring. There was still pockets of resistance in the Vukovar area, and there was still some fighting going on outside of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just briefly on the last page, paragraph 19 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The page is 0345, 0023, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "And General Panic orders that all units and formations, volunteers, local communes and so on, participated in combat operations in the territory of the 1st VO must be under the command of the JNA or else they will be disarmed and taken away while extremists will be arrested and appropriate legal measures will be undertaken."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The JNA had a plan that all the local units were to remain under the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But very soon thereafter, a new order followed pursuant to which they were to leave the composition. The orders followed one another very quickly. The situation changed at quite a quick pace, and this is correct here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll show you the orders. And paragraph 9, doesn't that really relate to paragraph 8 where they warn commanders about revenge by TOs and that TO units have already taken revenge? Isn't that an additional reason why they want to keep authority over those units? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander most likely knew why he wrote this and there must have been such instances in some areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And because of these instances, that's another reason why you want to keep control over those local units who aren't professionally trained like the JNA members; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not want to have them under our command following the liberation of Vukovar because objectively speaking, there was no need for them. Vukovar was free, and they went back to their peacetime location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: The fact that there were problems of revenge by local units and volunteers, wasn't that a factor in paragraph 9, to keep all local units under the control of the JNA? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph warns the commander not to -- commanders not to allow anyone to carry out any activities on their own in their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And isn't that another reason for paragraph 19, to keep all local units under the control of the JNA? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "All units and formations," and then in parentheses it says: "(volunteers, local units and others) participating in combat operations in the territory of the 1st Military District have to be under the command of the JNA." What they're warning about here is that they didn't want anybody to take the law into their hands. They wanted them to be placed under the command. That's how I'm interpreting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you received that document, the next notation relating to resubordination is in the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade, OG South, Exhibit 401 at 2.00 in the morning or 0200 hours on November 21st. Are you familiar with that or do you want to see that? Would it help you to review that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the document, yes. Based on the order of the commander of the 1st Military District, we produced our order, and I think that I signed our order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. That's Exhibit 422. "Four hours later an order was issued resubordinating the local TO and volunteers to the command of other JNA units." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that document -- may the witness be shown Exhibit 422, please. That's 03405685 to 56 ... If you see that order, that's your signature on the bottom, on behalf of Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what you state there is: "One, in the course of 21 November 1991, withdraw the Leva Supoderica volunteer detachment and dispatch them/resubordinate them to the 12 PMBR/12 K." That's what it says there. It's to be done during the course of 21 November 1991. And also at the top -- I'm sorry, right above that, it says: "Further to the newly situation and the order of the 1st Military District," you hereby order ... There is nothing in that paragraph or anywhere in this document referring to oral orders having been previously given; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you then signed it, signed that order on November 21st, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, should we break now or just continue on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have another quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the next document which came out is document 368, Exhibit 368 which is at 6.00 on the 21st of November, 1991, which is 03271248. Now, sir, this is a combat report. Did you prepare this or is that your signature there on behalf of the colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature is there. I personally am not the author but I signed it. This was produced by operations officers. My signature is at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in the -- this is at 6.00 on the 21st of November, and I just want to go through two paragraphs, the first one in relation to Ustasha forces. It says: "Ustasha forces did not open fire. There is a constant threat of fire from the remaining Ustasha forces." In that paragraph, are you referring to the remaining remnants or the pockets of resistance that still exist?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an objective threat posed by the forces that had hidden somewhere, and also from the forces that were infiltrated from outside, firstly in the form of a -- sabotage and terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at the end of paragraph 2, you state: "In the course of 21 November 1991, and further to your order, strictly confidential number 115-151 dated 20 November 1991: We have regulated all resubordination issues regarding volunteer units and returning the subordinated units back to their original structure." From that paragraph, you're indicating to your superiors that you are in the process of resubordinating all those units as they requested at 2.00 a.m. on the 21st of November; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you then signed it on behalf of Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the 22nd, there is another combat report where the resubordination of units are described. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 425. Now, this is another combat report from Operations Group South to the 1st Military District; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, again you state: "Ustasha forces in Vukovar didn't display any activities. There is a constant danger from the fire operations by the remnant Ustasha forces. Ustasha forces had massive defensive engineering works and they planted booby-traps in the facilities and buildings as well as the parts of weapons -- as well as on parts of the weapons and equipment." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So there was still a danger from remnants of the Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smaller groups, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it still is a problem for you, as the deputy commander, it's still a problem or a danger to your soldiers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Booby-traps and other types of mines and remnant forces were a constant threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2, you discuss Operations Group South, and you state -- do you see where it says: "In the course of the 22nd of" -- "22 November 1991"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "In the course of 22 November 1991, according to your strictly confidential order number 115-151 from 20 November 1991, all issues regarding the release and subordination of the volunteer units have been realised." That paragraph, sir, indicates in relation to the volunteer units, the resubordination was finalised on November 22nd, 1991, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's signed at the bottom of that document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see it right now, but I could see earlier that it was signed. If you were to scroll down a bit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was signed by Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's when he notified the 1st Military District, his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this report was sent to the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving away from that, sir, I've got just a few questions for you on another topic. Can an officer, sir, be resubordinated to a command without having command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer can be sent to work in another unit or in another command and can be given an assignment in that other unit or command. Yes, he can be sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Colonel Pavkovic. When he was sent to the Guards Motorised Brigade, which becomes OG South, you previously testified in Belgrade, which is the first time you ever mentioned him, that he received tasks. Would you agree that it was Colonel Mrksic who gave him tasks or orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Zlatoje Terzic, by means of an order of the Federal Secretary of National Defence produced and signed by the chief of cabinet of the Federal Secretary -- at the time that was Vuk Obradovic. So by means of that order, they were sent to the Guards Motorised Brigade. Colonel Pavkovic was sent to the command of the Guards Brigade until the completion of the mission, and Colonel Terzic was sent to the artillery organ of the Guards Brigade. Such an order exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When quoting the words of the witness from the Belgrade trial, Mr. Weiner said that Pavkovic -- that he stated there that Pavkovic had received tasks there, and the page in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- doesn't mention that. So perhaps it would be fair if this was put to the witness in its original form. There are some five to six relevant lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was just a general statement before I got into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Maybe then it's a convenient time for a general break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sounds good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm going to wrap it up, Your Honour, within 15 minutes. May the witness be shown Exhibit 404, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you, sir, the document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is the document you were discussing previously, the assignment of Colonel Pavkovic to the Guards Motorised Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you've testified that you can be resubordinated to a command without having command responsibility. Isn't it true, though, that Colonel Pavkovic could receive tasks or orders from Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pavkovic had a peculiar role. He worked with Operations Group South and had to be in touch with his own superior who had sent him there to begin with, which was the cabinet of the federal minister for All People's Defence. He could have taken his orders from the federal secretary through the cabinet, specifically from Colonel Vuk Obradovic, the chef du cabinet. He could have carried out assignments within Operations Group South pursuant to orders from Colonel Mrksic in as far as the cabinet was in agreement. In addition to that, the -- please allow for the possibility that then or now, I would not be able to say with any great precision what exactly the subordination system was that was in place between Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Mrksic. It was a peculiar situation, and they, I believe, would be best placed to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, may the witness please be shown MFI 763, please. While that's coming up - it takes a minute, sir - you've testified about a team being sent to Vukovar around the 20th, the 22nd, to look at the health situation, the dead bodies, those dead bodies that were out there. You said Colonel Basic was involved in this special team that went out there. Remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that a team was sent from the military medical academy led by Major Stankovic who, as we speak, is the present defence minister. At the time, he worked as a pathologist at the VMA, the military medical academy. He took a team to Vukovar for clearing the battleground. I also know at one time whether on the 22nd or the 23rd, Colonel Basic arrived in the area on orders from the command of the 1st Military District. His assignment, having something to do with the sanitization of the battleground, and I don't think it's a good idea to waste any more time now explaining what that's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could you look at the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report on the sanitization of the battleground and the Vukovar area as well as other areas at risk. This is the command of the 1st Military District sending a report to the Federal Secretary for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that document signed? If you can move it down, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was signed by the commander of the 1st Military District, Colonel General Zivota Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's also stamped.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it discusses that sanitization project which you were familiar with in relation to Colonel Basic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And have you ever seen the report that was issued? Did you ever see the report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen it. This was afterwards. They remained and kept working after we had left the area, and I never heard at any later time that they had made any kind of report whatsoever. Needless to say, they would have been expected to produce a report; the order says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is stamped, there's no question that this is a JNA military document; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you look at the next page in the B/C/S, which would be page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This page is only -- this document is only one page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is an MFI, Your Honour, this document was introduced by Witness Basic who was called by Attorney -- the attorney for Mr. Mrksic, and I believe it had to be translated but it should be in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's MFI 00763, and ours says 24 pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have it in English but not B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document in B/C/S is only one page long, while the document in English is 39 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have it on our screen in the e-court system, in B/C/S it's 24 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we need to proceed without that, Mr. Weiner. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the actual report discusses mines, booby-traps. Is that the type of issues that would be discussed in a sanitization report of an area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to a number of other things, this is also a report on booby-traps. You would find such subjects there as the losses or casualties or booby-traps. It very much depends on what the army commander had said exactly when he told him to go there with his team. Probably to carry out some engineering work, too, in addition to clearing the mines. I do assume that a rather complex report was eventually produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And within the report there's also discussion of the number of dead animals that were removed, the number of dead human beings that were found and removed, and plans for identification. Is that the type of information that you will find --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think by asking these questions, Mr. Weiner is asking the witness to speculate. He can't show him the document in the B/C/S and yet he's asking him to analyse the document that the witness has apparently never seen. I think Mr. Weiner is trying to achieve something with this document but the witness has already addressed the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness doesn't seem to be having any trouble answering. He indicated that booby-traps and mines were one type of subject that would be found within the report, and he indicated that there would be others. We have an extra copy of the report if the witness would like to see it. And I would like to continue to ask him some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Weiner. Pass the copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that this type of sanitization report would also involve issues of dead animals, dead bodies found in the area? Aren't those the types of subjects and matters that are provided within a report, a sanitization report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow, I think I would really need to take some time and read this carefully. But whenever you have a sanitization report, it should, as a rule, be a complex report addressing all the different subjects or any problems that one comes across. I would be hard-pressed to offer a valid comment unless given a chance to carefully go through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally would a sanitization report also concern clearing of rubble, residential building damage, and what is necessary to get the city going again or the town going again? Are those the types of subjects that are normally found within a sanitization report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that depends on the specific orders of the superior officer. And then the report encompasses everything that is set out in the original assignment. I think he was simply carrying out his assignments, and almost by default, this report was produced. If the commander of the 1st Military District had ordered for him to clear the rubble and clear the roads, bearing in mind the fact this was an engineering unit, among other things, then certainly this is something that should be reflected in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this report which was provided by Defence counsel, we would like to offer it. The letter which -- it is attached to is from General Zivota Panic to the Federal Secretary for Defence introducing this report, and it was provided by the attorney for Mr. Mrksic and we would like to offer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first something that I think concerns both myself and Mr. Borovic since our situation appears to be similar. The very method employed here to tender documents reminds me of me trying to get that Goran Hadzic video in through the back door sometime ago. Everybody recognised Goran Hadzic, but nobody knows what that's doing now so that's what Mr. Weiner is doing with the witness now. There is something else that is even more important, which is the reason I'm asking this be kept as marked for identification. The exhibit that Basic brought to the courtroom, it wasn't Mr. Mrksic's defence. What he had in frond of him, if you remember, and then Mr. Moore asked to have a look and then the document was marked for identification. What I'm concerned with and something I believe to be of great importance is this: The Sljivancanin Defence or the Radic Defence never set eyes on that document before it was seized from the witness, if I may put it that way. The document was not served on us in a timely fashion when we were still in a position to cross-examine. I believe we should be able to cross-examine him as the author of that document. Only then would we be in a position to say whether it should be admitted or not. He was a Mrksic witness here and the document was seized from him but we've never seen the document beforehand and the witness left. That's why I believe it should still remain as just marked for identification so that we could see whether we would be asking for that witness to be called again before the document is possibly admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, did you challenge the authenticity of that document when you came to deal with the witness after it had been put forward by Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It wasn't about the document at all. Nobody wanted to discuss that document in the courtroom. Mr. Moore asked for it to be Xeroxed and translated into English. I was in no position to challenge a document which was not discussed at all while the witness was still in the courtroom. The witness was never asked to analyse the document. We can go back to the relevant portion of the transcript and see what it's about. But as far as I remember, he had that document, Mr. Moore asked what's that document, and the document left the witness's hands and we, at the time, didn't even know what it was. We were unable to challenge the document or do anything else with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer is no. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I may be the one best placed to explain what happened with this, since the Mrksic Defence didn't originally use that document in our chief or on redirect, nor was the document on any of our lists of documents that we were going to use. Not a single question asked to the witness was based on that document, which is precisely what my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, has been talking about. Mr. Moore, towards the end of his cross, asked to see that document in front of the witness that was simply lying on the table, and that's when it was marked for identification. Even the Prosecution failed to ask the witness a single question about that document. My learned friends from the other Defence teams have never had occasion to see this document or indeed comment on it. The Mrksic Defence did not use this document while examining the witness as my learned friend Mr. Weiner has suggested. Photocopies were made of this document and, it was seized from the witness and yet we never asked the witness to say anything about that document. Therefore, I back this motion by Mr. Lukic. The document should remain an MFI document until its authenticity is confirmed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a military document. It is stamped. It has an attachment in that it was -- it has an accompanying letter from the general of the 1st Military District. It concerns Vukovar. It concerns a witness that was here. It concerns an issue or issues that have been discussed here. There is no issue as to its authenticity. It is relevant to the issues. We gave Defence counsel notice as to which documents we would use in cross-examination of this witness, and that was included, the Basic document. So based on its authenticity, its relevance, and reliability, we'd ask that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the first time, a witness has identified this document and confirmed its apparent authenticity for what it is on its face. There is no present reason to see it other than as relevant. In those circumstances, the Chamber will receive the document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will become Exhibit 763.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you went to the barracks in Ovcara -- I'm sorry, not the barracks, the farm at Ovcara, because it was necessary to go there. You were very interested on November 20th. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was necessary, and I felt responsible for the -- having all the information available in relation to my assignment or, rather, for being able to provide complete information to my own commander. I was told to go to that government session. I was there throughout. I went to Ovcara. I assessed the situation. I went back to the command post and I informed the commander. I thought that I was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You never returned to Ovcara after November 20th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You never went back there to see if there were any trials or to see what was happening with the prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for that day when I passed, only to realise that the trial had not even begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As necessary as it was to go there on the 20th, that you went out of your way to go there, you never returned, and I put it to you the reason you didn't return is because you knew the people were dead. You knew that those prisoners were dead.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I never returned was there were no more assignments there for me. The next day, I had an altogether different and very specific assignment, to organise a press conference, to receive about 120 domestic and foreign journalists who had arrived that morning. I'm talking about the 21st. They arrived in both Negoslavci and Vukovar itself. After that, we went about our own business, our own problems, the problems faced by the people there, how to make it possible for people to go where they chose to go. How to resolve all of these problems that they were now suddenly facing in a situation where the opposite side just refused to have them, more often than not. We also received orders to send our units back, and we were preparing our units for their return to the Belgrade garrison. We had a lot on our plate. We had a lot of problems, and I never received any assignments about Ovcara. Quite the contrary, in fact, my assignment was in relation to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you had a need to go there. You went out of your way to go there on the 20th. And you never went there again. Is it a coincidence that need or necessity to go there ended at the same time the lives of all of those prisoners ended?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I had no information to indicate what was going on with those people, nor did I have any assignment that involved them, nor did I feel that it was necessary, once my report to the commander had been submitted, for me to go back to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions of this witness. Your Honour, based on his statement where he is accepting the whole statement, it's our view that he has adopted his prior statement and we would like to admit that, would like to move the admission of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. I see Mr. Borovic would like to go first, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just one question -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought Mr. Borovic wanted to say something about this motion by the OTP but he actually had a question. I'm against the statement being admitted into its entirety. This is contrary to prior established practice. The fact that a witness stands by his statement does not necessarily mean that the statement should be admitted. Mr. Weiner talked about the amendments and changes that were made to the statement. I see no reason for us to now amend our established practice and for this witness [as interpreted] to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement will not be received in evidence, Mr. Weiner. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the reference number 855, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you had a point somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask a single question because my learned friend, Mr. Weiner, referred to this in his cross, so I believe that entitles me. The subject was resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're not entitled to any further questioning, Mr. Borovic. May I suggest you might have a quiet word immediately with Mr. Lukic while I finish making some notes. He may be able to help you in his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this is the first time that we are discussing this, all of the Defence teams believe that I was entitled to do that. But all right, so we understand each other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am the one who may have misled Mr. Borovic and that was certainly not my intention. But, Your Honours, I remember when we had a Defence pre-trial conference I asked you about the position of all the Defence teams, and you said that if a Defence team did not say anything to the contrary, then it had the status of examination-in-chief and that was the situation with Mr. Borovic, unlike Mr. Vasic who actually conducted cross-examination. So I believe that Mr. Borovic had the same status as I did. I raised an issue that had to do with Mr. Borovic's examination-in-chief, so I was the one who may have misled him and I will be the guilty one in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position is that normally co-accused stand as an examining party when they question another -- a witness of another accused. They don't stand as a cross-examining party. The position is different if there is an issue which has become the subject of direct conflict between the party calling the witness and the other accused or one of the other accused. In that situation, in respect of that subject which is the matter of conflict, the counsel for the other accused may cross-examine, and Mr. Vasic has taken advantage of that and has been allowed, of course, to do it. But that happens when the witness is being dealt with by that counsel. It's not a situation that arises after the Prosecutor has cross-examined in their position. Just to complete the picture, in case it might be relevant, always, there is the possibility that some matter has arisen by complete surprise at some later stage after counsel has questioned the witness and may seek leave to continue to reopen, in effect, their examination or cross-examination, because of an issue that is a matter of complete surprise that has arisen when some other counsel has questioned the witness. I don't think we are dealing with that situation now, but I hope those few words may have helped counsel to understand their various positions. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, good afternoon. I'm sure that you are tired of all of us here, and I will endeavour to ensure that you can return home as soon as possible. Let us try to cover these topics as briefly as possible. During the first day of cross-examination, if I may call it that, my colleague Mr. Vasic asked you about the operations log book, war diary. He also mentioned the war room where the documents are kept. My question is: Can any soldier or officer enter the war room and remove a document from there without observing a strict procedure, without anybody else knowing about this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are all documents in the war room kept under seal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the war room during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add this, the war room has several doors, it has bars, keys, locks. In front of it, there is a guard on duty 24 hours a day. The war room has, according to regulations, be on an elevated floor [as interpreted]. At the time, the war room was located in the then Bulevar Mira 22 where they used to be the cabinet of Marsal Tito, and this building was one of the targets during NATO bombing and is razed to the ground -- or was razed to the ground. According to some information we received, that area is to be cleared and a new U.S. Embassy is to be built there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic put to you paragraph 66 of your statement to the OTP as to whether, at the regular briefing of the 18th, the evacuation of the hospital was discussed, and I think that you clarified that in clear terms as to where the mistake occurred. Could we now please see Exhibit 402, B/C/S page 56, English page 1. This is the ledger. We also know that there was an order by General Panic for the hospital to be taken by 1000 hours on the 19th. It is marked 1614-8281. Now, let us look at an entry in the ledger. Is the ledger used to record the date and time when a document is received at the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, as well as when the documents are sent from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
