utterances.text: All right. Page 56. Could we please enlarge the upper left portion. Yes, this is precisely the section that we need. Entry 433. What date is it and to which document does it pertain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th of November, 1991 to the command of the 1st Military District, report on liberated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to be leading, but was this the report of the 1st Military District sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the name of the command -- this is the sender, so we are receiving this from the command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about entry 436?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 436 is something sent by the command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is dated 20th of November. It says here 1614-82/83, 19th of November. An order. Do I need to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Tell us, please: Was this ledger available to you when you gave your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the ledger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us move to a different topic. Mr. Vasic showed you document 442, Exhibit 442, which is the order of General Stojanovic from the 1st Military District banning any exchange of persons without his prior consent. You said that you were familiar with this document as well as the chief of security?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to slow down. If you remember, what was the position of Mr. Sljivancanin at the time concerning the exchanges of imprisoned JNA soldiers and officers in Croatia? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that there were imprisoned or rather blocked soldiers and officers in the barracks. It was in our interests and also this was required by our orders, to capture as many members of paramilitary formations so that we do exchange them for our men. This was very important for us to exchange them for our men, and we would give hundreds of enemy soldiers for one of ours. I can give you an example. For example, Relja Tomic was in the barracks in Gospic. He was badly beaten, and we barely managed to get him out alive, and we gave hundreds of captured soldiers in return for him. To conclude, all of us wanted to have as many captured soldiers for exchange as possible, and I can tell you that this was the main motivation for Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday, Mr. Vasic put to you a position whereby he claimed that it wasn't -- that it was impossible for you to hear from those present in the barracks that there would be a cabinet session held in Vukovar, and he was wondering how you could have known about this before the government actually arrived in Vukovar. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mrksic tell you then or later that Mr. Jaksic came to see him before the cabinet session and what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrksic didn't tell me that Jaksic had come to see him; however, I received that information from the people who were milling around the buses. They said that they had their own man who wanted to go and ensure that this would happen and that at the cabinet session this topic would be discussed. They wanted to make sure that they would be the ones trying these people, putting them on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic also told you that some members of the cabinet gave statements saying that the topics discussed at the session were not consistent with what you said and he wanted to hear your comment. You gave us your comment, and now I'm going to ask you this: He gave you no names. Do you know whether these people testified for the Defence in the Dokmanovic case and, if so, what would you conclude on the basis of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Defence case in the Dokmanovic trial, they attempted to shift the blame, all of the blame, to the army. The people who attended the cabinet session naturally testified in such a way as to protect themselves or people from their inner circle. However, I affirm what I said about what I had heard at the cabinet session, and I take full responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic also put a quotation to you of a statement by Goran Hadzic from that trial, where Hadzic said that his statement given on TV was for propaganda purposes. We heard that statement of his as well. My question is this: Did you know, did you hear later on that Goran Hadzic went to Sremska Mitrovica seeking to reclaim the prisoners that had already been taken there? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only heard his comment at the cabinet session when he said that in addition to not allowing that the prisoners be transported to Sremska Mitrovica, he would also request from the military authorities that those who had already been transported to Sremska Mitrovica be given back to them for trial, and they wanted to hold a trial and second-instance proceedings, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already said about that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he actually went to Sremska Mitrovica and whether he actually talked to somebody. All I know is that he said that he would go.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the people were taken to Sremska Mitrovica from Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 422 - no need to put it on the screen - that's an order that you signed on the 21st in the morning, at 6.00, about resubordination. And Mr. Vasic showed this to you at the time when you were working on this document with him. Do you remember whether it so happened that you yourself signed some documents even if Mr. Mrksic was present at the command. Were there such occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such occasions and documents. I think that there are such documents in the file. While preparing for my testimony, I saw a lot of documents with my signature, even if Mrksic was present, and naturally also when he wasn't present. It all depended on how urgent the document was. And it also depended on its content. There was nothing questionable about me signing a document since there would normally be an oral order before a written one ensued, an oral order from the 1st Military District, and there was sufficient basis for me to sign a document or an order. And as to why I signed it, well, most likely it was done in order to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a correction for the transcript, page 50, line 14. You said that there was an oral order and that following that, a written order came in.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see Exhibit 412, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the order dated 15th of November, 1991. Can you tell us who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. One of the copies of the order which I signed, you can see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the content, it should be similar to the other order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It has to do with resubordination, regulating the issue of resubordination by means of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up to see the date, to see the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the 15th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Mrksic was absent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him being absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now see Exhibit 414, please. This is a combat report dated the 16th of November at 1800 hours, could we scroll down to see the signature, please. Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the next day, isn't it? What does your memory tell you, was Mrksic away at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe there's something to show whether he was or wasn't in the war log, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to return to Mr. Vasic's questions at the end because there was a unified set of questions that he shared with the OTP. Now I'd like to address a specific question by Mr. Weiner. Last Friday on page 34 of the provisional transcript - I don't have the official reference, I apologise - he asked you whether Operations Group South or the Guards Motorised Brigade, on the 20th of November, had sufficient forces to neutralise any threats to the prisoners and your answer was yes. My question: On the 20th of November, 1991, did the 80th Motorised Brigade have sufficient forces to neutralise any possible threats to the prisoners at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade had sufficient forces. My answer was yes. Of course we did have those forces, but at this point in time, on that day, the 80th has that one task alone, to secure the hangar at Ovcara. And it has sufficient forces at its disposal. I can list them for you: Three motorised battalions, an anti-aircraft defence, artillery battery, and an anti-armour battalion, not to mention all the minor units, but these were the major elements. Then they had a local, a town commander who was appointed pursuant to orders of the commander of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic or anyone else from the 80th Motorised Brigade ask you on that day to provide any form of assistance in terms of equipment or manpower for the purpose of securing those people there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no assistance whatsoever was requested; at least none that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you. You don't know about the others, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any other requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner also asked you about the existence of civilian authorities in Vukovar or any of its bodies; you remember those questions, don't you? My question: In your opinion, when did the armed clashes in Vukovar stop?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thickest of the fighting ceased on the 18th of November, but there was still sporadic skirmishes. There was still sporadic skirmishes by minor groups that were soon neutralised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, under the rules applied in the armed forces of the SFRY at the time, the Territorial Defence were not involved in combat just under whose jurisdiction is it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When not involved in any combat mission, the Territorial Defence is sent back to its peacetime location and its peacetime duties. It is then under the authority of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned while testifying in chief, and I believe you said to Mr. Weiner, too, you knew at the time that the government of the SAO of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem were in Dalj. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, was it not expected that civilian authorities would be established in the now liberated Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the expectation. After all, that's why on the 20th, they had arrived in our area and passed themselves off as serious authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, how convincing were the speeches that the cabinet members made at the meeting in terms of these newly existing authorities in the area or their functioning.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sounded convincing. They said they had their own judiciary, their own courts, their own ministries, their own bodies. They said Vukovar was now free. They wished to thank us, but they would have those people and try them. They were so convincing, in fact, that I was 100 per cent certain about their intentions, and I was anxious to see how they would get the trials off the ground, how they would bring charges against people. I took at face value whatever they said. They left the impression of being a serious set of new authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember on those days in the media, TV news and such, were any facts mentioned in relation to that cabinet, to that meeting, to any action that they took?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Number one, there is no indication in any notice that's been given to the Prosecution of anything that's come out in the media, so I don't know what they're going to be discussing. And we never raised the issue during cross-examination of what was in the media in relation to that cabinet. We never raised the issue what was in Belgrade or anywhere else on the media in relation to that cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was raised in detail on cross-examination. Did this witness have any reason to believe that this -- these new authorities indeed existed. That was the subject and that's why I'm asking the witness whether he knows about any statements, public statements made by the cabinet members at the time for the benefit of the media. That is exactly what he was asked by Mr. Weiner on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may ask what basis the witness had for believing these governmental and legal resources existed but you shouldn't go on then to be suggesting yourself possible sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to raise in relation to what you have just said, Your Honours, but that's entirely different from what was suggested by Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, did word reach you at the time of the factual existence of those authorities -- of that cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were media reports to that effect, which I took note of. As I said, this government did not function in our area before the 18th, and we hadn't seen them until the 20th, at least I hadn't, but they did exist. They made statements to the media, and they worked in Dalj. They affected a lot of different developments but not in our area before the 20th. At least no influence that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm invoking some facts -- or, rather, Mr. Weiner was invoking some facts that you spoke about in your statement to the OTP about Sljivancanin. Mr. Weiner seems to believe that Sljivancanin did a lot of things that were outside his remit, outside what he was supposed to be doing. The fire adjustment is one thing that was raised. The war log appears to reflect that he personally informed General Panic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is a speech, Your Honour, and also it's not Mr. Weiner seems to believe, I was reading his statement. But this is -- there's no question here, this is just a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps, then, your objection is premature and you might be moving me to stop the speeches because of their effect on time, Mr. Weiner. But at the moment, I will be silent. Hurry up, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to hurry things along to not quote the transcript but rather summarise the main point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question is: What about those activities as to where the -- as to checking whether there was any sabotage or anything like that within the unit? Was that within the remit of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they said about the shortfall of the missiles, this is a security issue in as far as it relates to human lives. It also affects the morale. Thirdly, the progress of any assignment is in doubt whenever you are not sure about your own artillery. To round this off, I am entirely convinced that Major Sljivancanin did the right thing and that he wanted to make sure there were no acts of sabotage being carried out which was a matter of interest to him as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether him informing General Zivota Panic came with or without the approval of Commander Mrksic? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say either way, but I think it's very difficult for a major to just get in touch with a general like that, using a shortcut, as it were. He would need to obtain approval from his own commander, as a rule. So I would assume that Colonel Mrksic was aware of this and that he gave the nod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that, at least as far as you could tell, he was too much in the public eye. If you're not particularly well-informed, might that not lead you to believe that he was a more high-ranking officer than he actually was? To be more specific, did you hear stories to that effect told by people who were not exactly familiar with the set-up of the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just look at him, he's so tall, he's so brave, so good looking, you look at him, you see him in a certain situation and to an untrained eye, he might seem to be the commander. But all he did was his job, as well as some other people in terms of morale, in terms of logistics, as well as other things too. We did our best and we did more than we were required to do by our job descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You attended almost regularly meetings of the commander of Operations Group South. Did you at any point or from anyone hear about Sljivancanin giving orders to any units? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. No such comments, no such inferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me try to be even more specific, since we know that military police battalion commanders attended these meetings. Did you ever hear from Paunovic, Kavalic, or Susic about Sljivancanin interfering with their work or giving any orders to them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything about Sljivancanin interfering with the command in the 1st or 2nd Military Police Battalions. This is confirmed by the fact that the commanders came regularly to the command post to take their assignments, and the commanders of all the assault detachments and battalions were directly in touch with the commander on the phone so that at any given time, they would be able to receive their assignments or submit their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Weiner also asked you this: He asked you if you remembered the death of Sljivancanin's driver really shaking Sljivancanin leaving him very moved -- concern for other soldiers' lives. Is this something personal, is this something that is likely to get to you as a human being, or is that just another figure?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: War is a serious social phenomenon and I would say an instance of enormous human stupidity. People get killed in a war. What Sljivancanin was shattered by, what he was moved by, something that any of us would be moved by, the death of any soldier, any officer, all the more since Major Sljivancanin himself was at risk. His life was in danger. You must allow for the possibility that it wasn't easy to be Major Sljivancanin at the time, and objectively speaking he had to be every reason to be not moved but shattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about the atmosphere outside the hospital on the 19th, the commotion of those people assembled there was sort of subsiding and you were asked with why you'd never told anyone about that before. I raised an objection and the Presiding Judge told me I could ask you the question on redirect, so I'm asking you: Did anyone ever ask about that before you actually brought it up here in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the point was never brought up, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. The Prosecutor quite literally asked you whether you knew who Arkan was, and you said yes, you were familiar with the name from the media. You said that on page 50. Did the media say at the time that Arkan was killing for pleasure?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That objection is correctly made. Move on to the next matter, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question had to do -- or basically arose on the basis of Mr. Weiner's question. [In English] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us, please, what units mostly accompanied Arkan, what were his troops?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned this unfortunate Arkan, as I said to you, I saw him for the first time at the cabinet session. Papers wrote about him at the time, and perhaps they were biased describing him as a great man, great patriot. I didn't read that particular comment that he killed for pleasure but I knew that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is a question which has been sustained. That's not the -- the issue is who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Move on, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he went with the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not putting the same question. I'm asking him something quite different. I think that I can remain on the topic of Arkan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... something that's quite different and not the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, would you please answer my current question? The previous question was disallowed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As to which units accompanied him when he went fighting, he stood no chance, he had no desire, nor did he even try to be in our area of responsibility. He went to locations where some commanders accepted him or to places where the military discipline was loose. And he was close to General Biorcevic; they were good friends and brothers in arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the Chamber is informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Operations Group North on the other side of the Vuka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yourself that you would have arrested Arkan had he appeared in your area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have definitely been arrested by Major Sljivancanin and his organs of security because we did not allow such persons to stay in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 60, line 15, the witness said that General Biorcevic was the commander of the Operations Group North. And in my previous question, there is a mistake, page 60 line 13 and 14, my question is that I assumed that the Chamber was aware of what position was held by General Biorcevic and you explained that, so let us move on. Could we now have the break, Your Honours, so that I can review my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter to 6.00, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, we don't want to put to you the decision on resubordination dated the 21st of November, I'm sure you know it by heart by now. Mr. Weiner asked you towards the end whether in that decision it is mentioned anywhere that there was an oral order; you said no. My question to you is what -- do you stand by what you stated earlier, that there had been an oral order and from which time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A day earlier, there was an oral order, and following that order, it said that written order would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us move on to other topics. You spoke about the meeting. Mr. Weiner asked you why you didn't go to convey to Mr. Mrksic in the course of the meeting what direction the meeting was taking. Was Arkan active in the meeting? Did he discuss --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him say anything. Maybe he said something before I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm only interested in what you remember.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear him speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear, do you remember whether anybody mentioned any revenge? Did they say they wanted revenge or did they want to put these people on trial?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They solely spoke about putting them on trial, which is something that Hadzic himself confirmed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have before you your statements. Mr. Weiner put paragraph 71 to you. This is your statement to the OTP where you stated that: "Looking back, I now believe that such a surrender is not normal." So without looking back, would you please try to place yourself in the relevant period of time. The discussion you heard at that session, did it leave an impression that their requests were not normal, that what they requested was not normal? Is that the impression that you left with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that Vukovar was free, it was liberated, that the cabinet was in session, it was meeting, that it wanted to put on trial these people, I fully believed them, but I also have to reiterate that I wasn't competent for conducting any negotiations with them. I wasn't authorised to promise them any concessions either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you testified, page 63, Friday's transcript, you said that you wanted to go to Ovcara because you wanted to have full information about what followed after the cabinet session?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you convey to Colonel Mrksic full information that you had on that day, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I conveyed to him in true and accurate terms what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You sketched a map, the road leading to Negoslavci and the turn to Ovcara. Do you remember, from the intersection of the road from Vukovar to Negoslavci, from that intersection to the hangar at Ovcara, what's the distance?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a kilometre and a half at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't wish to interrupt Mr. Weiner on Friday, and thus I wish to state that on page 1446/17 there is a numeric error. The witness said that there was 7 to 8 metres, that that was how long the driveway or path leading to hangar was, and the transcript reflected 80 metres, or 800 metres, which was obviously unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner also asked you on page 72 of the draft transcript dated the 10th of November -- or, rather, he stated that you saw people attacking the buses in the barracks. Upon your return from the cabinet session, were there still any attacks on the buses, buses in plural, because you said that there were three to four of them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from the cabinet session to the barracks, there were two or three buses parked. Next to them was the security detail policemen, and then several officers. The situation was completely calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you set out to Ovcara, when you decided to stop by Ovcara, did you worry at the time about what was going to happen to those people or were you guided by your need to acquire full information? This question arises from what Mr. Weiner asked you at the end; namely, as to whether you could suppose that those people would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not even occur to me, and nothing indicated that there could be some revenge-taking. The main motive, the main goal for me going to Ovcara was to see whether the government cabinet had started functioning, and I wanted to acquire full information from my commander, so that I could convey to him upon my return to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew what forces the 80th Motorised Brigade had at its disposal on that day. Given the situation at the time, was Vojnovic able, as brigade commander, to freely use his units to implement the task?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Vojnovic, but in my view even the military police company commander was able on his own to reinforce the security personnel. Especially Vojnovic was able to use any other unit if there was a need to protect somebody or to intervene in a particular situation. On that day, he did not have any other task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he require any consent from Colonel Mrksic in order to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't need Colonel Mrksic's consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session, briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether the 80th Motorised Brigade had its own security organ and, if so, do you know who it was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade did have its security organ. However, I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't pursue this further then. You were asked by Mr. Weiner about Colonel Pavkovic. He said that you mentioned him for the first time at the Belgrade trial. He put to you whether you knew that he had certain tasks at the time. Would you please turn to page 74 of the Belgrade transcript of your testimony. For Your Honours and for my learned friends from the OTP, it's page 77.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They will bring it to you now. Page 74 for the witness. I will read it out slowly; it's a brief passage. It has to do with the questions put to you by Mr. Weiner at the time you were examined by the accused, Stanko Vujanovic. The question was: "Did you see Pavkovic on that day?" And then you answer: "Pavkovic?" And then Vujanovic says: "Yes." Your answer is yes. Then Stanko Vujanovic: "What did he have, what task did he have?" Your answer: "He had a specific task. He was a kind of an advisor there." "Q. To whom?" "A. To Mrksic. How could I explain his role now that you've mentioned him? The fact that he was there and that he performed many jobs both militarily and professionally from the surrender of that unit to the transport of the people and the surrender of the people who wanted to leave. They shot at him at some crossings and so on. He was there on behalf of the cabinet, because at the time he was in the cabinet of the federal secretary." So at the time, it was your judgement that Pavkovic was some sort of an advisor of Mr. Mrksic. But given what you testified, did you also have some memories of him doing something for the ordinary citizens of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned there, I said that he was of assistance there, and he mostly dealt with negotiations, meeting with delegations, sending the columns of people into various directions. He simply performed a useful job. It is difficult for me to explain the specific nature of the role he had and the relations he had with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you gave your OTP statement in July of 2005, did the OTP show to you any document of the European Monitoring Mission that I showed to you while proofing you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any such document. I saw the documents which were mentioned in my statement, my OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just those that are mentioned in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only thing that was put to me and that was appropriately recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you say roughly how many documents you were shown over those two days of being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly a total of ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can now discuss your statement to the OTP, and also what I really want to know about, what is stated there and what you have confirmed about you saying that Sljivancanin, in terms of command, was in charge of the evacuation. So we'll have a look at that. My question is: Your statement to the OTP, is it a result of you speaking informally, or is it actually a sequence of questions and answers from a purely technical point of view? How exactly was the statement taken?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the text book question and answer thing. If you look at the statement, at the final document, it shows that there are no questions as such, but there are thousands of answers. There were at least three times as many questions as far as I remember. There were questions or groups of questions that I used as a basis for my answers. I don't speak English myself; an interpreter was present. I signed the statement. The statement is valid in its present form, and that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, take any paragraph containing about ten sentences, can you remember how many questions you were asked in relation to the substance of a single paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can say that some of the questions were pretty clear-cut and aimed at a certain type of answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at paragraph 69 now that you have looked at already with the assistance of Mr. Weiner. I will read the first sentence slowly: "Mrksic also informed us at the briefing of the command in Negoslavci ..." I will wait for you to find that paragraph, paragraph 69.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Mrksic also informed us at the command briefing in Negoslavci on the 18th of November --"

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've said as much. Thank you. "... that Major Sljivancanin was going to be in charge of (command) the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th and 20th of November, 1991." Based on your recollection, did you say at the time that you took the expression "in charge of" to mean "to command" as your remark indicates in the parenthesis right there? Did you use the word "command" yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I looked at the original and the English, I made no changes in relation to this when I was entering all the changes and when I was meant to sign the statement. I accepted this, but I don't think this is my wording. I think this was added. This is more by the way of an inference on the part of whoever processed the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, when you signed the statement, you agreed with this, you raised no objections, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I made a lot of changes. And I think you've noticed yourself as you go towards the end of the statement, there are less and less changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 72. Again, just one sentence: "This implied that Sljivancanin was able to issue orders to the military police or any other unit participating in the operation." Paragraph 73, the next question. This is also something that Weiner showed you. "I do not know whether Sljivancanin issued any specific orders, verbal or written, regarding the organisation and implementation of the evacuation. He must have been issuing orders to the military police." Did you hear Sljivancanin issue orders to the military police on that day or did anybody tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't think I would state it this way again. I think there must have been something leading, a question or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's speculation, Your Honour. I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is perfectly proper. The answer may have involved speculation that will affect its weight, Mr. Weiner. Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll be going back to that statement later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, the theory of the OTP, as reflected in the indictment and their questions, is that Colonel Mrksic conferred upon Sljivancanin the command authority for the evacuation of the hospital. I'll now be asking you questions about facts and the actual situation that prevailed on that day. When you saw the bus from the hospital in the barracks which was, so to speak, at risk, did you inform Mrksic or Sljivancanin about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Commander Mrksic about that. And I ordered Lukic and Predojevic to send away any persons whose presence wasn't warranted and to make sure the bus was secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the hospital [as interpreted], did you inform Mrksic or Sljivancanin about the cabinet decision to take over responsibility for that bus and its passengers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 70, line 18, I didn't say at the hospital, I said, "After the government meeting," and you provided your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Colonel Mrksic told you to go to that cabinet meeting and tell them what you were talking about, did you inform Sljivancanin about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in touch with Sljivancanin until that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about that evening when you saw him, did you tell him about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you returned from Ovcara, did you tell Mrksic or Sljivancanin about what you had witnessed there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Needless to say, the commander, Mrksic, he was the one I informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Needless to say," you are saying now. And why didn't you inform Sljivancanin if he was the commander of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously Sljivancanin was not the commander, was he? It was Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know perhaps later that day, did you hear that on that day, a number of colonels from the security administration had been to see Mrksic about the -- their concerns over the people at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on that day, Susic, Captain First Class at the time, had called Mrksic to consult him on security issues in the barracks and previously had been at the command post when the evacuation was agreed? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that Susic, who was at the barracks, talked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know, since you were later that day you were at the command post in Negoslavci that anyone on that day at all addressed Sljivancanin about the civilian authorities or any threats posed to those people there, those persons there on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit 419, please. Can that be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown this, I believe by Mr. Vasic, if we could just pull that up a little. Vasic was showing you this. This is regulating issues to do with daily activities. The date is the 20th November. And this is the only written document with any reference to the evacuation. My question -- can we just pull it up a little, please, so that Mr. Panic can familiarise himself with the document. If you look at this document, is there a reference anywhere to any task for any organ of the command outside the functional competence or remit of anyone in the command of the Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this order to be perfectly proper. There is nothing in it that goes outside the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there any mention here of authority being transferred from anyone to anyone else, or conferred upon someone else?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not if I look at the face of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, Mr. Panic, on the 20th of November, what about the reports of subordinate units, and I mean the military police, first and foremost, who were they submitted to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All reports from battalions and assault detachments were submitted to the command post of the brigade or of the Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Panic, I have tried to count them, and so have you probably, you provided five different statements to different bodies and authorities about Ovcara. You provided an interview to the OTP; this took two days. You provided a statement as early as 1998 to the military court, and then that short statement to the security administration. You spent an entire day testifying at the Belgrade Ovcara trial, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of these five statements is also the one that I gave the Prosecutor in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Over these days, you've had an opportunity to thoroughly go through all your statements, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've said a lot of things about Ovcara. Did you ever tell anyone at all that Sljivancanin was in command of the hospital evacuation? Is this something you've remembered over the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I would be twisting the truth if I were to say that he was in command. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm about to complete my redirect, but I'll ask you another question through three questions. At the end of his cross-examination, Mr. Vasic told you that you were here to not tell the truth in order to conceal your own responsibility, to whitewash your own reputation. You gave an answer which still rings in my ears. You were told the same thing by Mr. Weiner at the end of his cross-examination. He suggested that you were here to conceal the truth and not to share it with us. Mr. Panic, were you not a potential witness for Mr. Mrksic's Defence at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did The Hague Prosecutor not inform you that they wanted you to appear as an OTP witness at this trial?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they eventually bring you here to testify or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I came here after meeting you, and I came here because I wanted to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much, Mr. Panic. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you will be pleased to know that that concludes your evidence and the questions you will be asked so that you are now free to go back to your other affairs. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here and for the assistance that you have given to us. The court officer will assist you to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Thank you very much for making it possible for me to take the stand before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ready to move on, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the next witness lined up and ready to take the stand, but I would like to take the opportunity now to raise that question which I announced at the beginning of the day. It will take about five minutes. This is what it's about, Your Honours. When you made the ruling regarding the possibility for the OTP to take interviews from Defence witnesses, after that we understood that decision to mean what it said. Over the previous period, at least that's what I know, Mr. Moore spoke to two Sljivancanin Defence witnesses in Belgrade. Two of the witnesses who were summoned or who were subpoenaed were returned. I was told this about a month or month and a half ago when I was in Belgrade myself. I really expected at the time, bearing in mind the fact that they have offices in Belgrade, the OTP would then and there get in touch with witnesses and interview them, Defence witnesses. I even asked Mr. Moore to give me notice of that so that I might organise for someone from my team to be there for the interviews. During the Radic Defence case, I noticed that when witnesses eventually arrived in The Hague, the OTP wanted to speak to them. Mr. Moore wrote to me on Thursday and talked to me on Friday morning expressing his desire to interview Mr. Korica, who has the meantime arrived, and Mr. Simic as well who has also arrived. We agreed for the interview to take place at 11.00 a.m. today and at 12.00 with Simic. He said that it would take no more than 45 minutes or up to 60 minutes for each of these two witnesses. I told him straight away that I wished to be present for both Korica and Simic's interviews. He did not agree to this, nor did he explicitly disagree, but the meaning I got from that, I gleaned from that was that he had nothing against me being present in my capacity as Defence counsel. When I brought Mr. Korica today, we sat down for the meeting, there was an interpreter, all the usual OTP procedures, Mr. Moore asked Witness Korica whether he would be prepared to give this statement in my absence. I was adamant that I should know the reasons for my presence being so in the way of Mr. Moore and his interview. Mr. Moore explained this by saying that he, himself, had not been present when I had conducted my interview with this witness and that this amounted to equality of arms and nothing else. Mr. Korica didn't oppose this idea of giving a statement in my absence, so I simply left the room. I do believe that taking a statement from a witness a day or two before the witness is due to appear, and especially in the case of witnesses who come to testify here, affects these witnesses in some way. I'm not talking about pressure. But really, just a single day before a witness is due to appear in the courtroom, to have an interview conducted without the Defence counsel present I believe is a fact that must be also considered in the light of the reason for these people coming here to testify. But the reason I asked to be present at this interview is this: I think Mr. Korica's interview took about two hours and Simic was not even interviewed today. There is one purely technical matter. We must now receive the record of that interview from the OTP. We have to read it and we have to analyse it with the witness before he takes the stand. I can hardly allow for a Defence witness to appear in court without previously going with him through the statement that he made to the OTP. If this goes on, and I do believe that I had to be there, and I do believe that Mr. Moore never needed to raise that subject for these very reasons, I will have no choice but to ask the Chamber for a postponement of that witness until I've had sufficient time to calmly go with the witness through his statement. I wish to comply with all our obligations before this court. I wish to comply with Mr. Sljivancanin's desire for us to finish our case by the 8th of December. If we go on like this, if I don't get the transcript tonight and tomorrow morning I will have to be doing that of all things, I just received a list with 85 documents that they wanted to show Korica today, well, then, I'm facing a situation in which I can no longer do what I had set out to do. This is no laughing matter, Mr. Moore. I think it's a very serious subject, and I for one am certainly quite affected. The OTP had two months, they had their own team in Belgrade, and now one day before the witness appears they wish to interview the witness. I had no choice but to inform the Chamber should a situation arise where I can't go with the witness through everything that he shared with the OTP, I will have to ask for a deferral, which is the last thing that I want to be doing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We went to Belgrade in September to speak to four witnesses; one of them was Mr. Korica. We had asked to speak to him. We were unable to speak to him in September. Mr. Korica has been here since Wednesday. The first time that we have been -- or he has been made available to us was today. My learned friend knew perfectly well that we wished to speak to him and, this is the only window that we were allowed to have. My learned friend has spoken, I believe, from what Mr. Korica tells me, has spoken to him on three previous days, starting last week. I have abided by the Court ruling. I have not made any fuss in court about having access to the witness earlier than today. My learned friend is correct that I asked Mr. Korica if he was willing to speak to us in the absence of Mr. Lukic. It was Mr. Korica's decision. The matter was fully tape recorded. My learned friend was there when that was done. He was present for the first 15 or 20 minutes of that. There is a tape recording which is being created into a format that will allow my learned friend to hear what was said. I hope that we can get it to him this evening, but this time table has not been of our making. The time table has been of the making of the Defence. In relation to the other matters of which I'm afraid I do not understand, where apparently there were two witnesses who were returned by us, I can assure the Court, as far as I'm aware, there were no witnesses returned by me; quite the reverse. I was in Belgrade to speak to the witnesses, not only in relation to Mr. Korica but also some others, and with regard to the case of Radic. I was unable to do that as the Court heard. So while my learned friend may object vigorously, there was absolutely no reason at all why we could have had access -- could not have had access from Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday prior to the weekend. My learned friend has been proofing Mr. Korica for three days. I have only waited until that has been concluded, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This man arrived on Wednesday. He is 70 years old. Mr. Moore came to speak to me -- or, rather, approached me on Thursday in writing and on Friday in person to talk to him, and it was then that we agreed to have the interview on Monday for an hour in my presence. The whole problem lies in the fact that I see no reason why Defence counsel should not be present when the interview is taking place one day before the witness is about to enter the courtroom. That is the contentious issue, Your Honour. Had I been present, I would have been able to take notes, I would not have needed the audio recording and I would have been able to speak to the witness immediately following that. The mail I received from the Prosecution was that they wanted to see Korica on Monday morning. That's the mail I received from them. And I don't see why my presence should be objectionable. Why can't I be allowed to sit there and take notes while the Defence witness is talking to the Prosecution? This is what surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just correct one matter, and it may be an oversight on behalf of my learned friend. We asked, in relation to this matter, the first time was on the 3rd of November in writing, having asked in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it written down as the 10th of November, but I think that this is not a material issue. What is important, however, is that such a technical issue should have been resolved much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is for a witness whether or not they wish to be spoken to by one party or another in the trial or are prepared to be spoken to in the absence of the other party, if I can confine it to Prosecution and Defence. And that is so with each witness and it will be so for any remaining witnesses to be called by Mr. Lukic which the Prosecution may seek to interview. If it is the case that the Prosecution seeks to speak to a witness some days before the evidence is to be led and the witness is here and not made available, then I'm afraid, in the situation of a trial such as this, the effect of that delay must tell against Mr. Lukic's position. The same would be applied in reverse were it a Prosecution witness and access to that witness was denied to Mr. Lukic. Therefore, it is clear that counsel need to be more attentive to the future need to speak to witnesses and to ensure that a witness is made available in reasonable time before the witness gives evidence if we are to avoid either disadvantaging Mr. Lukic or simply losing time in the trial. In the present case, we are prepared to accept that there was no conscious difficulty in the way of providing the witness and that some matter may have not been to Mr. Lukic's attention. If necessary, therefore, we would not continue sitting tonight and would continue tomorrow at the normal hour, which is 2.15, but that will not be the position we will take with future witnesses if there is any similar situation arising to the present. So the ball is in your court, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we -- the next scheduled witness is Simic, so we can bring in Mr. Simic and I hope that I will receive the transcript for Mr. Korica in due time. Mr. Korica is the next witness after Mr. Simic, so this is not a reason to delay the proceedings. We can bring in Mr. Simic right away because, after all, we have spent quite a lot of time with Mr. Panic. If I do receive the transcript in the morning, as Mr. Moore promised, and if we catch pace, then I do not envisage any problems in the future, and that's precisely what I wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore promised a tape, not a transcript, just so there's no lack of consistency and understanding. The witness, Mr. Simic, should be brought in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good evening. Would you read allowed the affirmation on the card given to you now, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening to everyone. Good evening, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You had to wait quite a while today. You had some problems because you came to have an interview with Mr. Moore which in the end didn't take place. However, the Prosecutor, Mr. Moore, apologised and I hope you will accept his apology.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, please give us your full name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Milivoje Simic, 15th of November, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you tell the Chamber and us what rank you hold and whether you are still an active serviceman and, if so, what is your post?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I am still in the active service of the army of Serbia. My rank is that of a colonel, and I'm currently commander of the 46th Logistics Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, would you please slow down for the sake of interpreters because everything is being translated into English, thus would you please wait for several seconds after hearing my question before you proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you commenced your military career, Mr. Simic, in 1982 when you completed military academy of the land forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: For a while, you worked in Skoplje, which is the capital of the one of the republics of the then federation of the SFRY, and now it is the capital of the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember from 1987 to 1990 where you worked -- did you serve in the military academy of the land forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: From 1987 to 1990, I served as commander of the cadet platoon within the military academy of land forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1990, pursuant to the dates that you provided to me, in August of that year you were transferred to the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: To the post of assistant for morale guidance in the 2nd battalion of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, according to the same data, you took over as deputy commander of the battalion and you served in that position during the Vukovar events for a while in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Further, according to the data, from 1993 to 1995, what were the posts you held?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: From 1993 to 1995, I served as battalion -- commander of military police battalion, first within the 46th Security Regiment, and later when it was disbanded and when the 46th Protection Motorised Brigade was established, I spent one year serving in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you also completed the staff academy?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the post of battalion commander in 1996, I went to the command and staff academy which I completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 2001, you completed the school of national defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I completed that school in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And in 2002, you took over the post that you just described just now as the post where you currently serve?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, initially it was the 46th Motorised Brigade. In 2002, it was renamed into 46th Logistics Brigade and this is where I currently serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I have to ask you to slow down, Mr. Simic. Based on the information you provided, in 1991, you served as deputy commander of the 2nd Military Police battalion and, according to the information available to us, you were not in that post throughout the entire time. So could you please explain to the Chamber how you went to Vukovar and what happened during the time period relevant to us, the 19th, 20th and 21st of November, 1991? What position did you hold at that time and how did you assume that position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The 2nd battalion of military police came to the Vukovar sector together with all other formations of the Guards Motorised Brigade; that is to say, on the 30th of September, 1991. Initially I performed that position, which was the establishment position, deputy commander of the military police battalion, but after some ten days, I became -- or, rather, commander of the 4th Company of military police became ill, that was Lieutenant Palmud Mesad [phoen]. Pursuant to the order of the battalion commander, Captain First Class Radoje Paunovic, I assumed the position of the commander of the 4th Company. From that time on until the 24th of November, that is to say, until our return to Belgrade, I served as commander of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Please tell me, were you and your company involved in combat and, if so, were you within another unit or did you fight independently?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When I took over as commander of the 4th Military Police Company, that company was resubordinated to the armoured battalion of the Guards Brigade and it was located at the Ovcara farm. In that sector, I spent some five to six days, roughly speaking, and then following that, the company was transferred to the Vukovar sector where, for a while, it was within the brigade reserve forces. Following that - I think we spent some three days there - the company was resubordinated to the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment, Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic. And up until the 17th or 18th of November, I can't recall the exact date when the order on disbanding assault detachments was issued, the company once again became part of the 2nd battalion of military police, and from that time on, it was subordinated to the commander of the 2nd Military Police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were part of the 2nd Assault Detachment, who was your superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When I was in the 2nd Assault Detachment, my superior officer was Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic, the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This situation that continued on the -- until the 17th and the 18th when you went back to your original unit, the 2nd Military Police battalion, on the 17th of November, or the 18th, from that date on, who was your commander, your superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: From the time the assault detachments were disbanded, it was the commander of the 2nd Military Police battalion, Captain First Class Radoje Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you take your orders from and your assignments?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean when I came back to the original unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the 17th and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: From the 17th onwards, the battalion commander, Captain Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Between the time you returned to your original unit, the 2nd Military Police battalion, and any later time, did you receive orders from anyone else but the battalion commander Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I received orders from the battalion commander alone and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I think that is beyond dispute. We all have a date here that we refer to as the date of the liberation of Vukovar, depending on your perspective. Obviously some say it was the date it was occupied. I'm talking about the 18th of November. Do you remember that date as the date you found out what occurred in Vukovar on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We learned on that day that the Croatian paramilitaries had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- they surrendered at Mitnica, right? So I'll ask you something else. Do you remember whether on the 19th of November you had any sort of assignment at all in the water-tower area or the Mitnica sector? If so, what sort of an assignment was it? What was the assignment? Who gave you the assignment? Did you carry it out?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether it was on the evening of the 18th or the morning of the 19th. The battalion commander told me to take the 4th Company of the military police and to search a section of the Mitnica neighbourhood. I can't remember the axis exactly, but I know that we left from Dalmatinska Street. The objective of this search was to, above all, establish whether there were any individuals or groups remaining there who belonged to the Croat paramilitary units. Another primary objective was to assist the civilians and to send them to the holding centre which I believe was located at Velepromet. That was the primary mission I received from the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, during that mission, did you receive another assignment? If so, from whom and what assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: As we were conducting this search, I was called by radio link by the battalion commander who told me to stop the search and to take the company back to the hospital area in Vukovar where I was to receive further assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do as you were told?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take your company to the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th of November, 1991? If so, do you remember what time it was when you got there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course I complied with the order that I got from my superior officer. As far as I remember, it was about 1400 hours that I reached the hospital sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, at about 1400 hours on the 19th of November when you reached the hospital sector, do you remember the numerical strength of your company, how many men were there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The initial numerical strength was over 100, and this was now down to 48 men, including me. That's why I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What were the reasons behind your numerical strength being so severely reduced, you had over 100 at the outset when you arrived in Vukovar, and now all you were left with was 48 men. Why?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There are several reasons for that: People were killed, injured, ill, the reservists were sent back. At the time, the JNA was a multi-ethnic force and my company comprised persons of various ethnicities. At one point in time, telegrams started arriving for soldiers increasingly telling them about the deaths of their close relatives, their fathers, their mothers. Because of these reports, we would allow the reservists to go back to their homes, after which they would normally not return to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the multi-ethnic make-up. Were there any Croats in the 4th Company of the 2nd Military Police battalion of which you were commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were Croats in my company, yes. My best soldier was a Croat. I'm not saying his name, just to keep him safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was he the only one or were there others too?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were several Croats. The first one to be killed was a Croat soldier, a lance-corporal. There were several Croats, Muslims, Macedonians, and of course Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, what about these persons of other ethnicities, were they actively involved in combat? I mean the Croats, the Muslims, the Macedonians.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like everybody else, all the other company men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm about to move on to the days that really matter. I hope my introduction was a brief one. I do believe, however, that we are running out of time. It might be a good idea to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have indeed run out of time, Mr. Bulatovic, and we will now adjourn until tomorrow. We resume at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 25
